source_text: Καὶ τὰ μὲν περὶ τῶν χρόνων διαφόρως πολλοῖς ἱστορηθέντα καὶ πρὸς ἡμῶν ἐκτεθέντα ὧδε ἐχέτω, ἑρμηνευθῆναι δὲ τὰς γραφὰς τάς τε τοῦ νόμου καὶ τὰς προφητικὰς ἐκ τῆς τῶν Ἑβραίων διαλέκτου εἰς τὴν Ἑλλάδα γλῶττάν φασιν ἐπὶ βασιλέως Πτολεμαίου τοῦ Λάγου ἢ ὥς τινες ἐπὶ τοῦ Φιλαδέλφου ἐπικληθέντος, τὴν μεγίστην φιλοτιμίαν εἰς τοῦτο προσενεγκαμένου, Δημητρίου τοῦ Φαληρέως καὶ τὰ περὶ τὴν ἑρμηνείαν ἀκριβῶς πραγματευσαμένου· ἔτι γὰρ Μακεδόνων τὴν Ἀσίαν κατεχόντων φιλοτιμούμενος ὁ βασιλεὺς τὴν ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ πρὸς αὐτοῦ γενομένην βιβλιοθήκην πάσαις κατακοσμῆσαι γραφαῖς ἠξίωσε καὶ τοὺς Ἱεροσολυμίτας τὰς παρ’ αὐτοῖς προφητείας εἰς τὴν Ἑλλάδα διάλεκτον ἑρμηνεῦσαι. οἳ δὲ ἅτε ἔτι ὑπακούοντες Μακεδόσι τῶν παρὰ σφίσιν εὐδοκιμωτάτων περὶ τὰς γραφὰς ἐμπείρους καὶ τῆς Ἑλληνικῆς διαλέκτου εἰδήμονας ἑβδομήκοντα πρεσβυτέρους ἐκλεξάμενοι ἀπέστειλαν αὐτῷ μετὰ καὶ τῶν θείων βίβλων. ἑκάστου δὲ ἐν μέρει κατ’ ἰδίαν ἑκάστην ἑρμηνεύσαντος προφητείαν συνέπνευσαν αἱ πᾶσαι ἑρμηνεῖαι συναντιβληθεῖσαι καὶ τὰς διανοίας καὶ τὰς λέξεις· θεοῦ γὰρ ἦν βούλημα μεμελετημένον εἰς Ἑλληνικὰς ἀκοάς. οὐ δὴ ξένον ἐπιπνοίᾳ θεοῦ τοῦ τὴν προφητείαν δεδωκότος καὶ τὴν ἑρμηνείαν οἱονεὶ Ἑλληνικὴν προφητείαν ἐνεργεῖσθαι, ἐπεὶ κἀν τῇ ἐπὶ Ναβουχοδονόσορ αἰχμαλωσίᾳ διαφθαρεισῶν τῶν γραφῶν κατὰ τοὺς Ἀρταξέρξου τοῦ Περσῶν βασιλέως χρόνους ἐπίπνους Ἔσδρας ὁ Λευίτης ὁ ἱερεὺς γενόμενος πάσας τὰς παλαιὰς αὖθις ἀνανεούμενος προεφήτευσε γραφάς. Ἀριστόβουλος δὲ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν πρὸς τὸν Φιλομήτορα κατὰ λέξιν γράφει· κατηκολούθηκε δὲ καὶ ὁ Πλάτων τῇ καθ’ ἡμᾶς νομοθεσίᾳ, καὶ φανερός ἐστι περιειργασμένος ἕκαστα τῶν ἐν αὐτῇ λεγομένων. διηρμήνευται δὲ πρὸ Δημητρίου ὑφ’ ἑτέρων, πρὸ τῆς Ἀλεξάνδρου καὶ Περσῶν ἐπικρατήσεως, τά τε κατὰ τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου ἐξαγωγὴν τῶν Ἑβραίων τῶν ἡμετέρων πολιτῶν καὶ ἡ τῶν γεγονότων ἁπάντων αὐτοῖς ἐπιφάνεια καὶ κράτησις τῆς χώρας καὶ τῆς ὅλης νομοθεσίας ἐπεξήγησις· ὥστε εὔδηλον εἶναι τὸν προειρημένον φιλόσοφον εἰληφέναι πολλά (γέγονε γὰρ πολυμαθής), καθὼς καὶ Πυθαγόρας πολλὰ τῶν παρ’ ἡμῖν μετενέγκας εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ δογματοποιίαν. Νουμήνιος δὲ ὁ Πυθαγόρειος φιλόσοφος ἄντικρυς γράφει· τί γάρ ἐστι Πλάτων ἢ Μωυσῆς ἀττικίζων; οὗτος ὁ Μωυσῆς θεολόγος καὶ προφήτης, ὡς δέ τινες νόμων ἱερῶν ἑρμηνεὺς ἦν. τὸ γένος αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰς πράξεις καὶ τὸν βίον ἀξιόπιστοι κηρύσσουσαι αὐταὶ αἱ γραφαί, λεκτέον δὲ ὅμως καὶ ἡμῖν ὡς ὅτι μάλιστα δἰ ὀλίγων.
pass_a_gloss: The things concerning the times having been narrated in different ways by many and also presented to us, let them be so, but the writings, both of the law and the prophetic ones, they say were translated from the dialect of the Hebrews into the Greek language in the time of King Ptolemy of the Lagus or, as some say, in the time of the one called Philadelphus, who brought the greatest ambition to this, Demetrius of Phalerum also having accurately dealt with the things concerning the translation; for, while the Macedonians were still occupying Asia, the king, being ambitious, considered it worthy to adorn the library in Alexandria, which was being made for him, with all writings and to have the Jerusalemites translate their prophecies into the Greek dialect. And they, still obeying the Macedonians, having chosen seventy elders, experienced in the writings and knowledgeable of the Greek dialect, sent them to him along with the divine books. And each one, having translated each prophecy separately, all the translations, having been compared, were in agreement in both the thoughts and the words; for it was God's will, having been deliberated, to be brought to Greek ears. It is not, therefore, strange that, with the inspiration of God, who gave the prophecy and the translation, a Greek prophecy, as it were, is being brought to pass, since also in the captivity under Nabuchodonosor, when the writings were destroyed in the time of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, Ezra, the Levite priest, having become inspired, prophesied, renewing all the old writings. Aristobulus, in the first of his writings to Philometor, word for word, writes; and Plato was also a follower of our legislation, and it is clear that he worked through each of the things said in it. The things concerning the exodus of the Hebrews, our citizens, from Egypt and the appearance and possession of all things that happened to them and the explanation of the whole legislation were translated before Demetrius by others, before the domination of Alexander and the Persians; so it is clear that the aforementioned philosopher took many things, having become very learned, just as Pythagoras also transferred many things from ours into his own dogmatic teachings. Numenius, the Pythagorean philosopher, writes straightforwardly; for what is Plato except Moses speaking in Attic? This Moses was a theologian and prophet, and, as some say, an interpreter of sacred laws. The writings themselves, trustworthy, proclaim his race and deeds and life; but we must also say, however, as much as possible in a few words.

pass_b_english: Let the various accounts of the times, narrated by many and presented to us, stand as they are; but the writings — both the Law and the Prophetic books — they say were translated from the Hebrew dialect into the Greek language during the reign of King Ptolemy Lagus, or, as some hold, under the one surnamed Philadelphus, who devoted extraordinary zeal to the project, with Demetrius of Phalerum overseeing the translation work in detail. For while the Macedonians still held Asia, the king, eager to adorn the library he was building in Alexandria with every kind of writing, deemed it worthy to have the Jerusalemites render their prophecies into the Greek tongue (2 Maccabees 2:13).

Since they were still subject to the Macedonians, they chose seventy elders, men skilled in the Scriptures and versed in Greek, and sent them to him together with the sacred books. Each translated every prophecy separately, yet when all the versions were compared they matched in both thought and wording; for it was God's deliberate will that the message reach Greek ears (Deuteronomy 4:6).

It is therefore no wonder that, by the inspiration of the God who gave the prophecy, the translation itself functions as a kind of Greek prophecy; just as in the captivity under Nebuchadnezzar, when the writings had been destroyed in the time of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra the Levite priest, moved by the Spirit, renewed all the ancient Scriptures by prophesying them anew (Ezra 7:10; Nehemiah 8:8).

Aristobulus, in the first of his books addressed to Philometor, writes word for word that Plato followed our legislation and clearly worked through each of its statements. Moreover, the account of the Hebrews' exodus from Egypt — our fellow citizens — and the manifestation and possession of all that befell them, together with the exposition of the whole Law, had been translated by others before Demetrius, before the rise of Alexander and the Persians; hence it is evident that the aforementioned philosopher borrowed much, having become widely learned, just as Pythagoras also transferred many elements from our tradition into his own system (Acts 7:22).

Numenius the Pythagorean philosopher states it outright: "What is Plato but Moses speaking Attic?" This Moses was a theologian and prophet, and, as some say, an interpreter of the sacred laws. The Scriptures themselves, trustworthy witnesses, proclaim his lineage, deeds, and life; yet we too must speak, as concisely as possible (John 5:46).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex historical and theological arguments of Clement. Pass A preserves the nuances of the Greek clauses, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering with appropriate scripture citations for the alluded content (e.g., 2 Maccabees 2:13 for the Septuagint tradition, Ezra 7:10 for Ezra's role). All clauses, including the comparisons to Plato and Pythagoras and the quote from Numenius, are accounted for.
